hero.alt: GlanceMap pairs a growing mind map with illustrations while the listener walks.
hero.caption: GlanceMap in use. The lesson shown is example study material.

sections.title: A mind map that grows with the audio
body: While walking, learners look away to check the path. The audio continues—and the connection between ideas can be lost.
GlanceMap pairs illustrations with a mind map that grows with the audio. Earlier ideas stay visible, so listeners can find their place again.
highlights: look away to check the path

sections.title: Learning on the go means looking away
body: AR glasses, a walking route, and a podcast that keeps playing. Causes, conditions and comparisons are hard to recover once the explanation has moved on.
Full captions preserve the words, but reading competes with watching the path. How can an AR interface help people attend to their surroundings and follow the explanation when they glance back?

figures.alt: Three moments along the walking route, with the crossing and pedestrian signal.
figures.caption: Walk and listen. Check the crossing. Return to the lesson.

items.title: Walk + listen
items.body: “I’m following the explanation.” Ideas arrive in sequence. AR glasses and earbuds deliver a podcast that builds one idea on the next.

items.title: Look away
items.body: “Is it safe to cross the road?” Attention shifts to the road. The audio continues.

items.title: Look back
items.body: “How did the podcast get here?” The listener missed how the ideas connect and must rejoin the current topic.

sections.title: Six goals, one final design
body: New ideas appear with the audio; earlier branches stay readable. Brief labels and familiar links make relationships easy to follow.
The map explains relationships. Illustrations ground concrete ideas.

figures.alt: GlanceMap’s final interface, connected by the three original dashed leaders to design goals one through six.
figures.caption: Reveal and retain context; keep labels and links clear; pair relationships with illustrations.

sections.title: An illustrated baseline for audio learning
body: Both prototypes used the same narration, illustrations and timing. GlanceMap added a persistent mind map.
Illustration Only builds on AudioXtend (CHI 2024). One of AudioXtend’s co-authors joined this project.

In AudioXtend’s earlier study with 12 people, adding illustrations improved recall by 33.3% immediately and 32.7% after seven days, compared with audio alone. These are prior-work results, not GlanceMap’s results.

figures.caption: Our AudioXtend-inspired baseline. This is not a direct test of the AudioXtend system.

sections.title: The study, on one shared route
body: Sixteen participants tried both formats on the same indoor route. Each heard four lessons, then returned for a recall test seven days later.

figures.alt: walking-route map, with six numbered markers and the author’s green route annotations.
figures.caption: Walk six indoor laps, take the escalator up, descend the stairs, and rejoin the loop.

figures.alt: masked photograph of the stair descent.

sections.title: Better recall, with attention redistributed
body: Free recall improved immediately and seven days later. Participants also found the lesson structure clearer (+1.59 on a seven-point scale).
Picture recognition fell by 7.1 percentage points. Better memory for the lesson came with poorer picture memory.
No detectable gait difference was found; workload showed a modest, model-dependent increase.

figures.caption: Immediate and seven-day free recall.

figures.caption: Picture recognition declined when the map was added.

highlights: Picture recognition fell by 7.1 percentage points

sections.title: Remember the structure. Give pictures enough room
body: Keep relationships visible, retain earlier context, and give important pictures enough room.

sections.title: Screen contrast alone cannot predict AR clarity
body: Alex starts with screen color rules. Through AR glasses, glare, visibility and meaning change.
The design needs to be clear (easy to see), comfortable (easy on the eyes), and meaningful (a color that fits the icon).

sections.title: The same people. Two lighting conditions
body: The same 20 people completed Studies 1–3. We used XREAL Air 2 Pro for the main tests, with a HoloLens 2 check.
Participants viewed randomized pairs, rated them and explained their choices.

figures.caption: Indoor experiment · 250–300 lux.
Outdoor experiment · 1,500–2,000 lux.

sections.title: Study 1 · Compare colors
body: Study 1 tested 12 selected hues with black, white and opposite-color letters: 36 pairs. Letter, size and stroke stayed fixed.
Clarity and comfort could favor different pairs.

figures.alt: The fixed letter T in black, white and opposite color.
figures.caption: The letter, size and stroke stay fixed. Only the colors change.

sections.title: Study 2 · Add meaning
body: Eight designers agreed on one icon per color. Study 2 retested the same 36 pairs with these meaningful symbols.
A clear color pair can still suggest the wrong meaning. Color needs to fit the symbol.

figures.alt: The twelve workshop-selected functions, each paired with its color.
figures.caption: Eight designers agreed on one icon per color. The same 36 color pairs were then tested with these icons.

sections.title: Study 3 · Refine and retest
body: Designers proposed shadows, gradients, outlines and gray backplates. We retested clarity, comfort, meaning and visual prominence.
Shadows improved clarity (+0.88–1.62); outlines improved meaning (3.71 → 4.13 / 5); gray backplates were least intrusive.

figures.alt: The designer workshop and its two refinement sequences: shadow and gradient; outline and gray background.
figures.caption: Workshop ideas became new edges and backgrounds, then returned to testing in AR.

sections.title: Match the design to urgency
body: Match the treatment to the icon’s role: draw attention, distinguish functions or keep status visible.

comic.title: Applying the AR guidelines
comic.caption: With these AR guidelines, Alex can design clear, comfortable icons with meaning that makes sense.
comic.alt: Alex walks outdoors with refined alert, music, dining, weather and file icons in her AR view
paragraphs: With these AR guidelines, Alex can design clear, comfortable icons with meaning that makes sense.

figures.caption: White icon + shadow. For information that needs attention now.
Colored icon + outline. Distinguish functions while more of the scene shows through.
Colored icon + gray backplate. Stay visible with less distraction. Backplate brightness: 30%.

sections.title: A gradient can change the message
body: The workshop explored hues ±30° apart. In the cyan comparison, blending toward green reduced clarity; blending toward blue raised it.
A brighter end can dominate. Keep both ends similarly bright, then retest clarity, comfort and meaning in AR.

figures.alt: cyan-green, plain cyan and cyan-blue examples with their observed clarity labels.
figures.caption: For cyan: cyan + green was less clear; plain cyan was the baseline; cyan + blue was clearer. Tested hue shifts were ±30°.

sections.title: Meaning depends on the audience
body: Bar and music colors evoked electronic clubs, mystery and cyberpunk. Blue–yellow parking recalled IKEA, competing with the parking meaning.
These guidelines cover 20 participants and static 2D icons. Test with the intended audience: culture, genre and context can change the reading.

figures.caption: Some participants found these bar and music colors youthful and stylish. Opposite colors were not always a poor fit.

sections.title: Six needs, one conversation
body: A future design concept: apply a palette to artwork, then refine it through dialogue. Six needs from the designer interviews guide the interaction.

steps.title: Clarify the brief
steps.body: “I’m truly torn over which colors to use.” — P23. Turn uncertainty into a clearer design intention.

steps.title: Set the context
steps.body: “Then I wonder whether this color existed in that historical context.” — P13. Ask for period and place before recommending colors.

steps.title: Compare palettes
steps.body: “It could give me a few more palettes to refer to, so I have more choices.” — P16. Offer distinct palettes shaped by the same brief.

steps.title: Explain the choices
steps.body: “For the stories and sources, I suggest adding a citation.” — P14. Explain meanings and link them to cited records.

steps.title: Apply to every part
steps.body: “Some of the other elements get ignored.” — P25. Preview the palette across all objects in the drawing.

steps.title: Keep judgment
steps.body: “It feels like compromising the design for this color.” — P16. Let the designer refine details or accept the result.

projects.title: Her Sound Re-sound
projects.subtitle: Who gets to tell her story?
projects.description: Rebuild Waner and Taiping’s shared memories, watch parts of their story disappear, then restore their political agency. A narrative puzzle about who gets to tell women’s history.

hero.alt: Waner and Taiping in the game artwork
hero.caption: Reclaim their past. Imagine our future.
hero.sourceOrigin: Original character art with the author’s Figma viewport

sections.title: Imagine our future
sections.body: Waner drafted imperial edicts; Taiping shaped court politics. Later accounts reduced their lives to scandal and rivalry. Play first, then question whose voices shape history.

items.title: Hackathon audience feedback
items.quote: We felt the strength of women here … and wanted to make games of our own.

figures.caption: Waner · Writing

sections.title: Build a shared memory
sections.body: The first scene shows the answer. Add Taiping to the banquet, then build the poetry scene yourself.

sections.title: Scroll to watch history disappear
sections.body: Six chapters become eighteen scenes. As you scroll, eight scenes dissolve. The gaps make the loss of their stories visible.

sections.title: Their lives become accusations
sections.body: Official histories tied Waner’s influence to sexual misconduct and accused Taiping of prolonging power. Later retellings made them romantic rivals. The game questions these inherited portrayals.

items.title: Old Book of Tang · vol. 51
items.body: Waner was accused of an “illicit affair with Wu Sansi.”

items.title: Comprehensive Mirror · vol. 210
items.body: Taiping was accused of acting “to prolong her power.”
